lesson.title: No Such Key: Understanding KeyError
lesson.summary: KeyError is what Python raises when a dictionary lookup asks for a key that was never stored, a different kind of missing value bug from IndexError even though both are common exception types.
lesson.body:
Dictionaries do not store items by position the way lists do, they store items by key, and each key maps to a value. That difference in how dictionary access works changes how the lookup can fail. A list index is out of range when a number falls outside 0 through len(list) minus 1. A dictionary key, on the other hand, is simply present or absent, there is no notion of a key being "too high" or "too low." When code asks a dictionary for a key it does not have, Python raises KeyError instead of IndexError. It is worth training yourself to see these as two separate bugs with two separate causes, even though both are common exception types you will run into constantly while working with real data.

```python
grades = {"Amara": 91, "Ben": 84}
print(grades["Amara"])
print(grades["Chen"])
```

grades["Amara"] finds a match and returns 91, printed without issue. grades["Chen"] has no matching key anywhere in the dictionary, so Python raises:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
KeyError: 'Chen'
```

Notice the message is just the missing key itself, in quotes, not a full sentence the way some other exceptions read. That can look sparse the first time you see it, but it is telling you precisely which key failed to match.

Unlike sequence indexing, dictionaries offer a built in way to sidestep KeyError entirely when a missing key is expected and not actually a bug: the .get() method, which returns a default value instead of raising.

```python
print(grades.get("Chen", "Not enrolled"))
```

"Chen" still is not a key in grades, so .get() returns its second argument instead of raising anything. Output: Not enrolled.

There is also the in operator, which checks membership without touching the corresponding value at all, as in if "Chen" in grades: before indexing normally. Choosing between .get() with a default, an in check, or letting KeyError happen and catching it, a technique the next lesson covers with the try-except block, depends on whether a missing key is a normal, expected situation or a genuine bug you want to know about loudly. Getting comfortable telling IndexError and KeyError apart on sight, from the traceback alone, will save real debugging time: one means the wrong position, the other means the wrong key.
